passages.title: Retention
paras: Every public body in an advanced democracy generates records faster than any institution can retain them indefinitely, and the determination of what survives is therefore not an archival question but a budgetary one. National archives respond to this accumulation through appraisal: a formal, documented process by which the records of an administrative body are examined and assigned a retention schedule specifying the period after which they are destroyed. The schedule is not a matter of local discretion. It is issued centrally, applied uniformly across every office of that body, and revised only on a fixed cycle.

Appraisal operates upon series rather than upon items. A file is appraised as a member of a classified group, and every member of that group receives an identical schedule. This design is deliberate. The individual assessment of each item would be prohibitively expensive and would in any case produce inconsistent results, since officers applying an unstructured standard would diverge from one another in the handling of borderline material. Consistency is obtained by removing judgment from the point of disposal.

Retention schedules are constructed around four tests. Material is retained permanently where it records the existence or constitution of the body itself; where it establishes rights or obligations, financial or otherwise, that may outlive the transaction to which they relate; where it documents the exercise of discretion, so that a decision might subsequently be reviewed; and where it possesses evident research value not anticipated at the time of creation. Where no test is satisfied, the material is scheduled for destruction at the earliest permissible date.

The apparatus is, judged by these criteria, sound. A test requiring that material be evaluated in the context of the decision it documents will, applied consistently, capture what later generations will require of it. The apparatus also provides for its own correction: schedules are reviewed upon a fixed cycle, and any office may submit a case for the retention of a specific series beyond its scheduled date.

It would follow from the foregoing that a record of unusual significance which a scheduled series had failed to capture would be recoverable through the review mechanism. The series is the unit of judgment; where the series has been scheduled, the individual item inherits that schedule, and the remedy lies not in the reconsideration of the item but in the reopening of the series. This is the position the system is designed to occupy, and it is the position its own documentation asserts.

passages.title: The Box
paras: I worked in records for twenty-six years, most of it at the county office, and the part of the job nobody warns you about is that you throw things away. That's the verb. Not transfer to offsite storage. Destroy. Twice a year a truck would pull up and we would load it.

The box in question came from the county clerk's office, the 1950s correspondence that nobody had ever requested in all the years I was there. Scheduled, routine, third week of October. I was on the cart with a clipboard. There were perhaps forty boxes that week and I remember most of them being boring.

I got to the clerk's boxes and one of them felt wrong, and I don't have a way to tell you what I mean by wrong. The boxes are all supposed to weigh about the same because they are supposed to be full of the same thing, which is paper of a uniform vintage, and this one was heavy the way a box is heavy when there is something in it that is not paper. So I opened it.

It was photographs. Several hundred of them, loose, not in folders, unnumbered on the reverse. They had been in an envelope, the envelope had come apart, and somebody in about 1958 had simply emptied them in and gone back to work. Buildings. Storefronts. A street with a tram line that is not there now. Hundreds of people standing in front of their own shops looking at the camera, and a date in pencil on about a fifth of them.

I did everything correctly and it made no difference whatsoever. I wrote it up, I flagged the box, I took it to my supervisor and explained the weight and the envelope and the photographs. And he was extremely reasonable about it. He said the schedule said destroy. I said the schedule said the test was research value. He said yes, and that was the end of it, because the series had been appraised and the series was county clerk routine correspondence, and photographs are not correspondence. There was no appeal. There is an appeal. I looked it up that night on the state library site, a perfectly reasonable-looking form, and the box went out on the truck on Thursday.

I still do not know whether I was right. Probably I was, and the town would have lost those photographs entirely within a decade if nobody had put them in a box at all. But that is not the same as the system working. The system did what it was built to do. I do not have a better phrase for what I did.

passages.title: What Ears Are For
paras: A female greater wax moth will not approach a hive. She will not approach a light, and she will not approach a hive that is warm and humming on a summer evening. She retreats, and she retreats fast, and the reason is that the wax moth is a parasite of the bee colony, and the moth's most reliable cue to a suitable host is a high-frequency sound that the human ear cannot detect at all. The moth responds to ultrasonic frequencies as high as three hundred kilohertz, which is beyond the hearing of every bat yet measured.

That single capacity is unremarkable to an entomologist and startling to everyone else, because it inverts the expectation that an animal's sensory range ought to be a function of its size. The moth is small. Its range is enormous. Nothing about its anatomy demands the upper limit; what demands it is the requirement that the moth detect the thing that is hunting it, and the appropriate solution, over a very large number of generations, was to extend the range until the predator's signal fell comfortably inside it.

The same logic, examined across a wider range of animals, produces a set of figures that at first appears arbitrary. The pigeon, which navigates over hundreds of kilometres and has no need of high frequencies, tops out at ten kilohertz. The barn owl, which hunts in total darkness and locates its prey by rustle, is more sensitive at the low end than almost anything measured and is equally uninterested in the high end. The elephant, which communicates across distances at which a visual signal would be useless, occupies the infrasonic band that a human being experiences not as sound at all but as a pressure felt in the chest.

Materials scientists studying the cochlea have taken a particular interest in this variability, for the reason that a biological system which has solved the same problem several hundred times independently has almost certainly found more than one good answer. The human cochlea is not the optimal instrument for detecting sound; it is the instrument that was adequate to the ancestors of a species which needed to hear speech, and to hear it well enough to locate a speaker in a quiet landscape. It is heavily invested in the two or three kilohertz band where the formants of human speech lie, and comparatively neglected everywhere else. The barn owl's cochlea is not a better ear. It is a differently shaped answer to a different question.

The traditional account of sensory evolution held that complexity of structure produced range, that an animal with a more elaborate auditory apparatus could therefore perceive more of the spectrum. This account does not survive contact with the wax moth, whose auditory system is small and lightly built and which nonetheless exceeds every vertebrate in the reach of its upper limit. The account that has displaced it is narrower and, in the estimation of most workers, considerably better supported: an animal hears what it must hear, and the shape of the organ follows the shape of the requirement.

The difficulty with the narrower account is that requirements are not always knowable in advance. An owl has no use for the upper frequencies, and will not acquire them unless the ecosystem in which it hunts changes in a particular way. A pigeon will not extend its range because nothing in its current life calls for it. A species can therefore be perfectly well adapted to a world that then ceases to be the world, and the range that was an advantage becomes a boundary that cannot be crossed from inside.

This is the sense in which the wax moth is not a curiosity. It is the one case in which an insect has been pushed outward along a sensory axis by pressure from a predator, and it has been pushed further than any vertebrate. What the comparison with the bat establishes is not that moths hear better, which is a meaningless question, but that the ceiling of the audible spectrum is set by ecological circumstance and is therefore not a constant. It moves. It has moved, repeatedly, in the direction of whatever was hunting.

passages.title: Somewhere to Sit
paras: Put two benches side by side and the difference is obvious before either has been sat upon. One has a flat wooden slat seat, four metal legs, a back, and a weight that makes it difficult to move. The other has a single concrete form, a slight backward tilt, an underseat gap of about ten centimetres, and a division down the middle that a person cannot sit across without appearing to intend to occupy two places. You will not have to be told which of these was installed to be sat upon for a while.

That both designs are recent, and that the second has largely displaced the first within two decades, is the part of the story that is genuinely difficult to explain, because the second is not cheaper. A cast concrete bench with a central division costs more to manufacture and more to install than a slatted timber bench, and it is considerably heavier. The change cannot be accounted for by economy, and it was not the product of a decision to produce fewer seats. Seat numbers in most public spaces have not fallen.

The furniture of a park is designed, in the ordinary course of business, by landscape architects, and it is specified through procurement documents, and it is installed by contractors who are working to a schedule. A design that discourages a particular use can enter the world without anybody deciding that it should. It enters the way a shelf height enters the world. Somebody working from a standard, a supplier offering a standard, an authority accepting a standard, and at no point in that chain a question being asked about what the standard is for.

The division down the middle of a concrete seat has a name in the trade, and the name is not decorative. It is a dividing bar, and it exists to prevent a person from lying down. The gap beneath the seat exists to prevent a person from sleeping. Both features are documented in municipal procurement schedules, described functionally and without euphemism, and both have been adopted broadly and without controversy, which is the remarkable part: there was no vote, no consultation, and no occasion on which anyone was asked to decide that a person lying on a bench in a public park was a problem requiring a hardware solution.

The consequence is that a substantial quantity of public seating has ceased to be seating in any meaningful sense and has become, in effect, a surface. It remains furniture, it remains in the inventory, and it continues to be counted in assessments of amenity, and the count is accurate while the description is not. The bench is still there. What has been removed is the permission, and permission was never a thing anyone believed was stored in the concrete.

This matters most to those for whom a bench is not a convenience but a necessity, and the population for whom that is true is not small and is not, in the main, visible to the people who commission benches. A person waiting for a bus, unable to stand, is not a person the concrete was designed for. A parent with an infant and no other adult. An old person for whom the division makes the seat too narrow for comfort rather than merely uncomfortable. Each of these is a person who requires a flat surface of a particular width, and each is invisible in a procurement document that records seat dimensions rather than seat use.

It is tempting to conclude from all of this that the modern bench is a failure of design, and that better design would resolve it. That conclusion is available, and it is not, I think, the more useful one. The bench has not failed. It has performed, and what it has performed is a purpose, and the purpose was achieved so efficiently that the achievement is now invisible to the people who commissioned it and unremarkable to the people who live beside it. What we are looking at is not an error in the making of something but the ordinary operation of a system doing exactly what it was built to do, and the difficulty is that this is what the making of things has come to look like when nobody is in a position to say no.

passages.title: The Slots Nobody Fills
paras: I schedule clinic appointments, which is a job that sounds like data entry and is actually about the distribution of pain across a Tuesday. I have done it for eleven years, at a mid-sized outpatient practice with nineteen providers, and I am responsible for a book roughly nine hundred appointments deep. The book has holes in it. That is the entire subject of this passage, and I want to be precise about what I mean, because nobody in my profession talks about it the way I am about to.

A no-show is an appointment that is not kept and not cancelled, and it costs the practice the full slot value, which for a new-patient visit in our building is one hundred and thirty dollars of clinician time alone. We run a fourteen percent no-show rate on standard follow-ups and nineteen percent on new-patient visits, which means we lose about four thousand two hundred appointments a year. A slot lost is not a slot that moves; it is a slot that becomes empty and cannot be refilled, because the patients who book earliest take the earliest slots and the ones who cancel late are the ones who wanted it most. In the last full year we turned away one thousand and ninety patients for lack of an available appointment, and we did that while operating at seventy-nine percent capacity. Seventy-nine percent of the book is not full. It is a book with holes shaped like the hours that people cannot attend.

The standard explanation is that patients forget. The reminders go out, some of them go to numbers that are disconnected, some of the patients are notnative speakers, some of the reminders require an app, and forgetting is the residual category that absorbs everything the system has failed to account for. I have heard this explanation given as though it were a finding. I do not think it is a finding. I think it is the sentence we say at meetings, and I have never once been able to test it, because nobody has ever measured whether the patients who miss appointments know that they had one.

We measured it this year. We took six weeks of data and asked, at the point of the missed slot rather than afterward, by telephone, one question: had you known you had an appointment today. Of two hundred and forty patients who had missed a booked appointment, one hundred and fifty-eight said yes, they knew perfectly well. They were not forgetful. They were present, informed, and did not come. Of those, just under half cited transport, a substantial number cited a childcare arrangement that fell through, and a substantial number said something closer to they had arranged their day around coming and could not arrange their day around coming. They knew. Attendance was not the variable. Attendance was the outcome of a set of constraints, and the constraints had not changed, and our reminder system had not noticed.

What we changed was not the reminders, which were already elaborate. We changed the book. We moved a hundred and forty appointments a year out of eight-thirty and one-fifteen, which are the worst slots in the building, into the middle of the morning, where the bus route is frequent and the parking is unrestricted and the walk from the car park is short. We allowed a fortnight's notice by text for anyone who asked for one, which costs nothing and is cancelled at a rate of under four percent. We closed the book to new booking at four-thirty on the day rather than at five, which recovered sixty-one appointments a year. None of these are innovations. Any practice doing this work has arrived at some version of all of them.

The improvement is real and I would not want to overstate it. We went from fourteen percent to nine. That is five points, and five points is about three hundred appointments a year, and three hundred appointments is a clinic that sees the people it turned away. But nine percent is not four percent, and I have no explanation for the residual nine that is better than the explanation I had before, and I have stopped pretending that the six-week telephone survey generalized. The honest position is that I know what the numbers are, that I know roughly why a third of them happen, and that I have a great deal less idea about the rest. Anyone who tells you they have solved this is describing their own data badly, and the surest sign of it is that they have a single reason.
